https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ukraine-w.text: Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Updated Tue, 28 July 2026 at 3:52 am UTC 0 Voldoymyr Zelenskyy said the drone display organised by Vasyl Goncharuk, pictured arriving in court, ‘certainly should not have taken place there’.Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images A Ukrainian court remanded in custody the organiser of a weapons exhibition that was struck by Russia in an attack that killed at least 11 people. Prosecutors brought a case against Vasyl Goncharuk, head of the Armada weapons industry association, accusing him of negligence leading to loss of life after the Russian ballistic missile strike on a shooting range outside Kyiv on Friday. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it “certainly should not have been taking place there”. Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it hit the site during “a demonstration of Ukrainian and foreign-made” drones. Goncharuk appeared at the Kyiv court limping and said he sustained light injuries in the attack. Prosecutors have said the weapons association invited more than 300 people including military personnel , state representatives and business figures without official authorisation, providing only a small shelter. The event was even promoted on social media. Agence France-Presse said its reporters saw homes in ruins and victims in body bags after the attack. Previous incidents of Russian attacks on openly held Ukrainian military gatherings have also triggered outcry and resignations. A Wildberries warehouse in the Koledino district of Moscow was reportedly on fire on Tuesday morning after being hit by drones as the Russian capital came under attack . The distribution complex for the Amazon-like chain had been targeted previously. A steel factory in Chekhnov, Moscow oblast, was also hit, the Kyiv Independent reported . The Russian regional governor, ‌Andrei Vorobyov, said an apartment ⁠building in Chekhov was damaged. Drones targeted other areas including ​Podolsk, ‌Domodedovo and ​Kolomna. The Pentagon official tasked with building ⁠a domestic drone ​industry said on Monday the US was still far behind Ukraine’s production capabilities . Travis Metz, chief operating officer of the Defense Innovation Unit, told Reuters that Ukraine would produce 6m-7m small first-person-view attack drones ​this year – roughly 500,000 a month. By comparison, the ‌Pentagon’s $1.1bn programme will have ordered ‌just under 200,000 altogether by February. But the US would catch up and lead the sector, he predicted. The Pentagon is insisting military drones must be made with US parts to foster “a wholly domestic” supply chain. None of the drones from the 19 companies competing an August test event may contain banned parts like Chinese-made ​motors or battery packs. “It’s an increasingly difficult thing,” Metz said. Ukrainian companies competing in the test, called Gauntlet II, are being required to localise production in the US as a condition of future orders. All ⁠100 members of the US Senate have been invited to ⁠a meeting ⁠on ​Tuesday evening with Volodymyr Zelenskyy . Ukraine’s president will be in Washington for the funeral of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a strong and influential supporter of Ukraine. A Senate aide ​said voting might also begin during Zelenskyy’s visit on a bill to impose sanctions on Russia that was championed by Graham. Zelenskyy is due to meet on Tuesday with Donald Trump. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war in Ukraine has changed dramatically. The Guardian’s Luke Harding looks at who has the advantage in the war now and how Zelenskyy’s strategy has shifted. Andy Burnham welcomed Zelenskyy in his first meeting with another world leader since becoming the UK prime minister , writes Pippa Crerar. “It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” Burnham said Britain was providing new jamming technology to Ukraine that would “help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives”. The system is known as Stone Cloak . Zelenskyy posted that he was “grateful” to Britain for “today’s decision to provide Ukraine with electronic warfare technologies” that would “certainly be useful on the battlefield”. Romania’s ⁠foreign ministry ⁠said it had expelled a ⁠diplomat at Russia’s embassy after repeated violations of ⁠its national airspace by ​drones. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots have shot down three drones in as many days. The Russian ambassador was shown drone fragments that Romanian authorities identified as a Russian “Shahed model” . Two people were hurt in May when a drone smashed into an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galati near the border with Ukraine. Ukraine ⁠struck a Russian export ⁠terminal in ⁠the Rostov ​region , as well ⁠as oil facilities in ⁠the Yaroslavl and ​Udmurtia ‌regions, Zelenskyy said on Monday. “Last night, our long-range sanctions were effective in the Rostov region. An export terminal approximately 250km (155 miles) from the frontline was hit,” he posted. “Deep strikes also targeted oil facilities in the Yaroslavl region and the Udmurt Republic , which is 1,300km from Ukraine ’s state border.” Five people were reported killed in Russia’s Rostov region bordering Ukraine. Russian ⁠forces meanwhile struck three Ukrainian ports, including ⁠fuel ⁠loading and ​storage facilities at the port ⁠of Odesa, ​the defence ‌ministry in Moscow said ‌on Monday. Related: The Ukrainian startup taking the missile fight deep into Russia Russian strikes on frontline localities in eastern Ukraine killed ⁠seven people and ⁠injured ​more than 20 on Monday, officials said. Prosecutors in the Donetsk region said three people died ⁠in two areas near the contested city ​of Kostiantynivka. A fourth person was killed near Kramatorsk, a heavily defended “fortress” city considered critical to Ukraine’s defences. Prosecutors said a total of 18 people were ‌injured throughout Donetsk region. In Ukraine’s adjacent Dnipropetrovsk region, the governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said three people were ​killed and six wounded in more than 50 drone and artillery attacks on five districts. Two people died near the town of Nikopol and one ​person was killed near the town ​of Syneklykove. Over ​the border ​in Russia’s Belgorod region , a Ukrainian drone struck a building, killing one person and injuring two. Donald Trump’s administration has told members ⁠of Congress it will not finish spending $400m in aid to Ukraine until fiscal year 2029, even as Kyiv runs critically low on weapons. Democrats and some ​of Trump’s fellow Republicans have criticised the Pentagon for sitting on aid for Kyiv that members of both parties pushed through last year. In May, the Pentagon sent a letter to lawmakers outlining its spending ⁠plan. It covers $200m for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9m for vehicles, spares and equipment and $100m for services such as transportation of defence articles to ​Ukraine. The funds still have not been put to use. https://www.dw.com/en/troops-from-north-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Itee A museum in North Korea honors soldiers who have fought for Russia Image: KCNA/REUTERS Advertisement In late 2024 , North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine . International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine .. Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia . Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region. North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Defense in Russia Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh. "These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv." Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory. The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression." "Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts." Russia has spread terror in Ukraine with rocket attacks on civilian targets Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS Russia not outgunned Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight. "If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces." Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report . Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025. In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two parents and three children. The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted. Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror." 'Instruments of terror' Ukrainian military sources say North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy. The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles. Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on . Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply. This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath." No turning point None of the experts DW spoke with believes that North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine. Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine. Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said. Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," Fyodorov said. This article was originally written in Russian. https://www.dw.com/en/spain-asks-eu-s-fr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JbMf Some Ceuta residents have attacked tents set up by the migrants along the beach Image: Antonio Sempere/AFP Advertisement Spain has asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing migrants who crossed into Ceuta last month and still remain in the North African Spanish territory. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska sent a request to Beate Gminder, the European Commission's director general for migration and home affairs, to help with screening migrants in Ceuta. Madrid has also requested 10 more Frontex officers to help with the screening. Frontex is the European Union agency responsible for managing the bloc's external borders and fighting cross-border crime. Why is Spain asking for help with the Ceuta migrants? Over 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco to Ceuta illegally in late July. The incident triggered a massive EU migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism. Though the majority of people were quickly sent back to Morocco, at least 5,000 migrants still remain in the Spanish territory of roughly 80,000 residents. Madrid cannot deport the remaining migrants quickly as a collective return without individual assessment is prohibited under international law and Spanish court rulings. Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Rising anger against migrants in Ceuta Ceuta's residents loudly reject the migrants' continued presence and have made their voice heard via protests which have sometimes turned violent. Spain has ruled out moving the migrants into the mainland as that would invite further criticism from the opposition as well as some EU members. Migrants have set up camp on Trampolin Beach, where some tents have been attacked and set on fire amid the residents' rising anger. On Thursday, protests turned violent with 12 migrants arrested after stoning an army vehicle, injuring one soldier and other migrants. Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that 11 migrants were expelled from the territory, citing sources from the city's main court. Photo: facebook.com/igsu.situatiideurgenta Sorin Iordan , 07.09.2026, 13:50 The Romanian firefighters who served for two weeks in Serbia returned home on Saturday after working alongside their colleagues from the neighboring country to battle wildfires that affected vast areas and entire communities. As part of this mission, Bucharest mobilized both a ground unit consisting of 69 firefighters and 15 pieces of equipment, as well as an S-70M Black Hawk helicopter, which is part of the European rescEU reserve, a capability hosted and operated by Romania through the General Aviation Inspectorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The aircraft participated in aerial firefighting operations, supporting ground crews and helping to limit the spread of the fires in the affected areas. “It was an intense two weeks, with complex operations, long hours of work, and difficult field conditions, but also with new experiences,” reported the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations. During the operations, Romanian firefighters formed two-person teams with firefighters from Serbia and Germany. The Romanian rescue team’s mission in Serbia took place through the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism, following a request for international assistance from the authorities in Belgrade. The extreme drought that has ravaged European countries has caused severe wildfires in Greece again this year. A new contingent of 40 Romanian firefighters arrived in Greece last week. They replaced their colleagues who had been responding to and monitoring high-risk areas during the last two weeks of August. During this period, the Romanian firefighters participated in specific missions coordinated by Greek authorities, as well as in training sessions and joint exercises alongside Greek firefighters and French partners. At the same time, they conducted field reconnaissance to familiarize themselves with the area’s characteristics and specific risks, according to the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations. The new contingent is continuing the mission with the support of two specialized vehicles for fighting forest fires, with capacities of 3,000 and 5,000 liters, one high-capacity vehicle with a 10,000-liter capacity, a 30,000-liter water tanker, a first-response and command vehicle equipped with a drone system, a shortwave radio communications vehicle, a minibus, a container truck, and an off-road utility vehicle equipped with firefighting equipment. This is the third contingent of Romanian firefighters deployed in Greece this summer and the sixth consecutive year that Romania has responded positively to Athens’ request for assistance. This year, Romanian rescue teams also participated in an international mission in southern France to support local authorities in fighting wildfires. They were praised both at the European level and by the French for the professionalism they demonstrated under extreme conditions.
